text.title: Competitive Intelligence Core Rules
text.summary: Seven rules governing a period-over-period CI brief: how a delta is proven, which false positives must be controlled for before one is recorded, what polling cadence a source earns, how hiring signal may be read, and when a delta may be promoted to a theme or an implication.

rule.statement: Every row in `deltas` carries before/after values AND two retrievable captures with distinct `observed_at` timestamps — an archive.org snapshot URL, a stored HTML/WARC capture, or a dated screenshot. A delta asserted from one current fetch plus recollection is rejected.

rationale.source: Internet Archive Wayback Machine — snapshot provenance

rule.rationale: Pricing pages, changelogs and homepages are mutated in place, not versioned. Once the vendor edits, the "before" value is unrecoverable, so an unarchived delta can never be re-verified and cannot survive the first challenge from a sales rep who saw a different number.

rule.statement: Before a pricing delta is recorded, refetch with a clean session (no cookies, no referrer), from a second geo/currency, and on the second billing period; the artefact records which controls were applied. A difference that disappears under any control is logged as `not-a-delta`.

rationale.source: Stripe Adaptive Pricing / Paddle localised-pricing docs + split-testing practice on pricing pages

rule.rationale: Vendors serve geo- and PPP-localised prices and run split tests on the pricing page. Both produce a value that differs from last cycle's capture without any pricing decision having been made, so an uncontrolled diff reports the competitor's experiment bucket as a strategy change.

rule.statement: Each monitored source declares a polling cadence no slower than its own publication rhythm — changelog/release notes weekly, pricing page monthly, job boards biweekly, filings and funding on event. A source polled slower than it changes is flagged `sampled` and its deltas may not be worded as "the change".

rationale.source: Sampling theory — aliasing below the Nyquist rate

rule.rationale: Two opposing edits between polls cancel: the competitor ships a price rise and reverts it, and the cycle reports "no change". The brief is then confidently wrong rather than uncertain, which is the worse of the two states for a downstream pricing decision.

rule.statement: A job posting may support a claim about direction and timing only — role, team, technologies named in the JD, posting date. Every hiring-derived implication states an expected lead time (req to GA typically 2-4 quarters) and never asserts that the capability exists.
rule.rationale: Reqs open before design is settled, many are backfills, and a large share are never filled or are quietly closed. Reading a req as a shipped feature builds a roadmap reaction to work the competitor abandoned, and the reaction ships before the competitor's does.

rule.statement: An entry in `themes` requires at least 2 deltas drawn from at least 2 different source types (e.g. changelog + hiring, not two blog posts). A single-delta observation stays in `deltas` and is not promoted.
rule.rationale: A lone delta from one surface is indistinguishable from vendor noise: a copy edit, a marketing test, an SEO rewrite. The theme layer is the part readers act on without re-checking, so admitting single-source noise there makes the whole brief unfalsifiable.

rule.statement: Every `implications` row names the specific decision it changes (a price point, a roadmap item, a battlecard line, a partnership) and the numeric trigger that would flip it. "Monitor closely" and "keep an eye on this" are rejected values.

rationale.source: Jan Herring — Key Intelligence Topics (KIT) framework

rule.rationale: Intelligence not tied to a named decision-maker's decision accumulates cycle over cycle and gets re-derived next cycle at full cost. Without a trigger value, no one can tell whether this cycle's brief changed anything, and the CI programme degrades into a newsletter.

rule.statement: Emit a structured skip when: fewer than 2 competitors have monitorable public surfaces; there is no prior-cycle artefact AND no archived capture to build a baseline from (run competitor-analysis first to establish it); or the only sources are auth-walled or NDA-bound.
rule.rationale: This methodology is a delta methodology. With no baseline every field reads "new", the output degenerates into a first-pass description of the market, which is competitor-analysis's artefact — and it will then be mistaken for a change report next cycle.
